analysis.one_liner: Gives college athletes the right to earn endorsement money, keep scholarships through graduation, and get sports-injury medical bills paid.
analysis.headline: The bill won five Senate Democratic sponsors but never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Judiciary Committee when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules of college sports in favor of the athletes who play them. It would bar the NCAA, conferences, and universities from stopping athletes from earning money from their names, images, and likenesses, guarantee scholarships until graduation regardless of injury or performance, require wealthy athletic programs to pay athletes' out-of-pocket sports-injury medical costs for years after eligibility ends, and put independent medical staff — not coaches — in charge of return-to-play decisions. It would also create a federal Commission on College Athletics to enforce these rules, funded partly by fees of up to $50 million a year on the largest athletic associations and conferences.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes — including foreign athletes on student visas — gain the right to earn endorsement money without losing scholarships or eligibility, guaranteed scholarships through graduation, paid medical care for sports injuries (2 to 4 years after eligibility ends, depending on the school's revenue), independent second opinions, freedom to transfer without penalty in defined circumstances, and a new federal ombudsman and hotline to report mistreatment. Women athletes gain Title IX equity evaluations published publicly each year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: College athletes, especially at big-money programs

how_it_helps.text: Bars colleges, the NCAA, and conferences from restricting athletes' ability to market their names, images, likenesses, or athletic reputations, and counts that earnings as separate from financial aid so it cannot reduce scholarships or federal aid eligibility [S3].

Requires universities with $20 million or more in athletics revenue to pay athletes' out-of-pocket sports-related medical expenses for 2 years after eligibility ends, and those with $50 million or more to provide portable primary health insurance and cover 4 years [S3].

Guarantees an athlete's scholarship for every year of enrollment until they earn a degree, regardless of athletic performance or permanent injury, with only narrow exceptions for academic misconduct or a sub-2.20 GPA for two consecutive semesters [S3].

Puts medical personnel and trainers under an office independent of the athletic department and gives physicians unchallengeable authority over return-to-play decisions, so coaches cannot pressure injured athletes to compete [S3].

Requires annual public Title IX equity evaluations in athletics, bans sex discrimination in comparable sports' medical care, facilities, and promotion, and requires annual public reporting of athletic program revenues, coach compensation, athlete time demands, and academic outcomes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The NCAA and major athletic conferences, which could be charged fees of up to $50 million a year in the aggregate and face fines and a new federal regulator; universities with large athletics revenue, which must cover medical costs, guarantee multi-year scholarships, publish program finances, and accept limits on restricting athletes' earnings; and colleges' existing business partners, which are barred from representing athletes if they have deals with the college.
analysis.who_pays_short: The NCAA, major conferences, and wealthy athletic departments

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state laws governing athlete earnings, agent regulation, transfers, and professional drafts, overriding the roughly thirty state NIL statutes already in force [S3].

It creates a new federally chartered Commission on College Athletics with broad power to write rules, certify and decertify agents, audit athletic departments, issue subpoenas, and set penalties, funded by a $50 million annual appropriation plus fees on the largest athletic associations [S3].

The compliance and medical costs fall on athletic departments, which could strain budgets at schools below the revenue thresholds or push costs toward students; the bill restricts eliminating any athletic program until coach salary, administrative, and facility cuts are exhausted [S3].

Some provisions would codify practices already underway — athletes have been permitted to earn endorsement money since 2021 — so the bill's incremental value beyond the status quo depends on enforcement provisions the NCAA and universities resisted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the athletes — who generate billions in revenue for their schools and conferences while bearing the injury risk — the protections are substantial and the direct cost to them is nil. The real costs are institutional: a powerful new federal regulator, preemption of state laws, and significant new medical and scholarship obligations on wealthy programs. An honest supporter would concede the commission design is expansive and that smaller athletic programs outside the revenue thresholds get few of the benefits. On balance, the bill is a clear transfer of bargaining power from athletic departments and the NCAA to athletes.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2022, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or advanced it, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the College Athletes Bill of Rights on August 2, 2022, with Senators Blumenthal, Schatz, Wyden, and Padilla as original cosponsors [S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The NCAA, major conferences, and high-revenue athletic departments keep the existing arrangement in which athletes cannot be compelled into medical coverage guarantees or scholarship terms by federal law, and no federal regulator oversees athletic departments.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The NCAA and big athletic departments

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the College Athletes Bill of Rights in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Richard Durbin (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: National Collegiate Athletic Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal legislation mandating athlete compensation and medical terms and pressed Congress instead for a law limiting athletes' earning rights and shielding the association from antitrust suits.

sides.party_line_note: All five Senate supporters were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors, and the bill received no Republican support before it stalled.

industries.note: The bill strips the NCAA and conferences of their power to restrict athletes' earnings, charges associations with over $200 million in annual revenue fees of up to $50 million a year combined, and subjects them to fines, audits, and a new federal regulator. Athletes gain exactly what these associations would have to give up.

Departments with $20 million or more in athletics revenue would have to pay athletes' out-of-pocket sports-injury medical costs for years after eligibility ends, guarantee scholarships through graduation, publish program finances and coach pay, and lose the right to revoke aid over endorsement deals. These are the schools whose football and basketball revenue the current system redistributes to coaches, facilities, and administrators.

industries.industry: NIL marketing agencies and athlete agents
industries.note: The bill locks in and expands athletes' right to hire agents and group-licensing entities and bars colleges from arranging or steering deals, enlarging the agents' market. But it also makes the new commission the mandatory federal certification body for athlete agents and lets it cap fees and revoke certification.

industries.industry: Apparel, broadcast, and sponsorship partners of college sports
industries.note: Companies that license athlete images would need group licenses before using athletes' names, images, or biometric data, and universities' business partners are barred from representing athletes — but the bill simultaneously protects brand deals that pay athletes directly.
